answer.evidence: The main body is the nave. Its large sloped roof plane (rows ~12-100) is drawn as dark shingle rows with diagonal beams and a light edge line along the ridge and the gable rafter. This counts as a roof top surface (c). The south gable wall below it (rows ~63-159) has a round window, arched windows and a door, so the front face is well over 3 rows. The right wing also shows a stepped roof slope. The bell tower on the left is drawn almost entirely as a vertical face, with a ruined, broken crown. Its top shows only dark back-wall brick and no front-edge line or eave shadow, so one major part has no clear top. The overall structure still reads as three_quarter because of the large roof plane.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a whole building (tower, nave with broken roof, door, windows), so it matches the reference kind. Its stone walls are shaded brick by brick in about 5 purple-brown steps, with lit edges on the broken roof and rubble. The roof slates carry per-tile variation, and moss, vines and grass tufts add more texture. The outlines are dark purple-brown, tinted toward the stone and not neutral black. Only 17% of dark edge pixels are near-neutral, so this is not a sticker outline. Measured facts: 23 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10 for the references, and 6% near-flat coverage, which comes from the dark window and door openings and is low enough not to count as flat fills. By eye it is at least as dense as the references and does not look thinner or flatter.

The tower has a broken top at rows 2-9, which reads as a dark masonry band ending in a bright rim. The roof is a sloped plane, evidence (c), so the structure is three-quarter.
